'''''Plumeria''''' ({{IPAc-en|p|l|uː|ˈ|m|ɛ|r|i|ə}}), commonly known as '''frangipani''', is a [[genus]] of flowering plants in the family [[Apocynaceae]]. Most species are deciduous shrubs or small trees. They are native to the [[Neotropical realm]] in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northwestern South America,<ref name="POWO" /> but are often grown as ornamental plants in tropical regions, including Florida, Hawaii, South America south to northern Argentina, southern China, northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Senegal, and in parts of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] with irrigation.<ref name="POWO" />

== Description ==
[[File:Frangipani without leaves W IMG 3624.jpg|thumb|Frangipani trunk in [[Kolkata]], [[West Bengal]], [[India]]]]
[[File:White Plumeria Flower.jpg|thumb|White plumeria flower in [[Coorg]], [[Chikmagalur]] ]]
Plumeria branches are [[Succulent plant|succulent]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Succulents in the Genus Plumeria |url=https://worldofsucculents.com/genera/plumeria/ |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=World of Succulents |language=en-US}}</ref> The trunk and branches of ''Plumeria'' species have a milky [[latex]] sap that, like many other Apocynaceae, contains poisonous compounds that irritate the eyes and skin.<ref>[http://www2.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/OF-24.pdf College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR). Ornamentals and Flowers. Feb. 1998. OF-24.]</ref><ref name="WH">{{Cite web |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/plumeria/ |title=Plumeria |last=Mahr |first=Susan |date=2023 |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |publisher=[[University of Wisconsin-Madison]] |access-date=15 February 2023 }}</ref>

=== Leaves ===
[[File:Leaves I IMG 8331.jpg|thumb|Leaves]]
[[File:Plumeria fruit.jpg|thumb|Fruit]]

''Plumeria'' species are small trees or low shrubs. The leaves grow at tips of their branches. Various species and [[cultivar]] have various [[Glossary of leaf morphology|leaf shape]] and [[phyllotaxis|arrangements]].<ref name="WH"/><ref name="IHoSP"/> The leaves of ''P. alba'' are narrow and corrugated, whereas leaves of ''P. pudica'' have an elongated shape and glossy, dark-green colour. ''P. pudica'' is one of the everblooming types with nondeciduous, [[evergreen]] leaves. Another, semi-deciduous species that retains leaves and flowers in winter is ''P. obtusa''; sometimes known as "Singapore plumeria".<ref>{{Cite web |title=NParks {{!}} Plumeria obtusa |url=https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/3/0/3072 |access-date=2024-05-05 |website=www.nparks.gov.sg |language=en}}</ref>

=== Flowers ===
[[File:Time-lapse of a Plumeria (Frangipani) flower opening.webm|thumb|Time-lapse of a flower opening]]
''Plumeria'' trees flower from early summer to fall. Their blossoms grow in clusters on ends of the stems, they are made of tubular corolla with a length of {{Convert|2-4|in|cm}} that split sharply into five rounded and waxy petals that overlap each other. These flowers come in many colours including pink, red, white and yellow, orange, or pastel. They have separate anthers.<ref name="WH"/><ref name="IHoSP"/>

The flowers are highly fragrant, especially at night. Their scent is perceived to have floral elements of [[jasmine]], [[citrus]], [[gardenia]], fruity aromatic notes of [[coconut]], [[peach]], [[vanilla]], as well as [[Milk|lactonic]], woody accords. However, they yield no [[nectar]]. Their scent tricks [[Sphingidae|sphinx moths]] into pollinating them by transferring pollen from flower to flower in their fruitless search for nectar.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Pollination by deceit in a mass-flowering tropical tree ''Plumeria rubra'' L. (Apocynaceae) |journal=Biotropica |pages=269–275 |volume=16 |number=4 |year=1984|jstor = 2387935|last1 = Haber|first1 = William A.|doi=10.2307/2387935 |bibcode=1984Biotr..16..269H }}</ref>

Its fruit separates into two follicles with winged seeds.<ref name="IHoSP"/>

== Taxonomy ==
The name ''Plumeria'' was first used by [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] in 1700, but was not formally published until 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]]. Linnaeus affirmed the name in his seminal work ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', and added the three species that were known at the time, ''P. rubra'', ''P. alba'' and ''P. obtusa''.{{R|LINNAEUS}}

Within the family [[Apocynaceae]], ''Plumeria'' is placed in the subfamily [[Rauvolfioideae]], tribe Plumerieae and subtribe Plumeriinae. The subtribe also includes the genera ''[[Himatanthus]]'' and ''[[Mortoniella]]''.{{R|ENDRESS}} The [[type species]] ''P. rubra'' was designated in 1925 by [[Nathaniel Lord Britton]] and [[Percy Wilson (botanist)|Percy Wilson]]{{R|IPNI}}

===Etymology===
The naming of this genus is attributed to French botanist [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] who, in 1700, created the name in honour of [[Charles Plumier]]. Plumier was also a French botanist, who had explored the tropical Americas as [[Louis XIV]]'s royal botanist, and described a large number of species.{{R|ZUMBROICH|p=342}}

===Common names===
The plants of this species are commonly known as frangipani in English,{{R|SGA|NPSING|ZIMING}} although the generic name ''Plumeria'' is often used as a vernacular name. Other names exist across southeast Asia in the various cultures, including ''kemboja'', ''bunga kubur'', ''chempaka'', pagoda tree and ''camboja''.{{R|NPSING}}

A fictitious account of the origin of the name 'frangipani' was published in 1867. The English perfumer [[George William Septimus Piesse|Septimus Piesse]] claimed in his book that the name is taken from that of a crewman with [[Christopher Columbus|Columbus]] by the name of Mercutio Frangipani. Piesse further claimed that Frangipani was able to detect a fragrance as the ship approached Antigua, and upon landing found it to be coming from the flowers of ''P. alba'', which was in bloom at the time.{{R|PIESSE}} This story and the Frangipani character were concocted by Piesse and some associates to drive up commercial interest in his products.{{R|ZIMING}}<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kettler |first1=Andrew |date=April 2015 |title=Making the Synthetic Epic |journal=The Senses and Society |volume=10 |pages=5–25 |doi=10.2752/174589315X14161614601682 |s2cid=192944557}}</ref>

== Propagation ==
Plumeria can be propagated by seed or vegetatively propagated by cutting stem tips in spring, allowing them to dry at their bases, then planting in well-drained soil. These are particularly susceptible to rot in moist soil. Applying [[rooting hormone]] to the clean fresh-cut end will enable callusing.

Plumeria cuttings can also be propagated by [[grafting]] to an already rooted system.<ref>{{cite book |first=Sharon H. |last=Thornton |title=The Exotic Plumeria (Frangipani) |publisher=Plumeria Specialties |year=1985 |page=21}}</ref> The Plumeria Society of America lists 368 registered cultivars of ''Plumeria'' as of 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://theplumeriasociety.org/registered-plumeria/ |title=Registered Plumeria |publisher=The Plumeria Society of America |access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref>

== In culture ==
[[File:Plumeria Floral Garland.jpg|thumb|Plumeria is commonly used to make [[Lei (garland)|lei]]s in Hawaii.]]

In [[Mesoamerica]], plumerias have carried complex symbolic significance for over two millennia, with striking examples from the [[Maya civilization|Maya]] and [[Aztec]] periods into the present. Among the Maya, plumerias have been associated with deities representing life and fertility, and the flowers also became strongly connected with female sexuality. [[Nahuatl]]-speaking people during the height of the Aztec Empire used plumerias to signify elite status, and planted plumerias in the gardens of [[Pipiltin|nobles]].{{R|ZUMBROICH|p=351}}

''Plumeria rubra'' is the [[National symbols of Nicaragua|national flower of Nicaragua]].

Plumerias were introduced into the Philippines in the 1560s by the Spanish, and from there they were taken into [[Indonesia]] and [[Malaysia]]. In these areas, plumerias are often associated with ghosts and death, and are planted around cemeteries in the belief that the fragrant flowers ward off evil spirits by masking the smell of decay.{{R|ZUMBROICH|p=357}}<ref name="MB">{{cite web |last=Bautista |first=Norby |title=The summer blooming of the Kalachuchi |url=http://www.mb.com.ph/the-summer-blooming-of-the-kalachuchi/ |website=Manila Bulletin |date=22 April 2015 |access-date=19 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150531011259/http://www.mb.com.ph/the-summer-blooming-of-the-kalachuchi/ |archive-date=31 May 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Yangsze Choo in her novel ''[[The Night Tiger]]'' for example described it as is "the graveyard flower of the Malays". Plumerias often are planted on burial grounds in all three nations. They are also common ornamental plants in houses, parks, parking lots, and other open-air establishments in the Philippines. Balinese Hindus use the flowers in their temple offerings. The plumeria's fragrance is also associated with the ''[[Kuntilanak (folklore)|Kuntilanak]]'', an evil vampiric spirit of a dead mother in Malaysian-Indonesian folklores. In the culture of the Philippines, this vampiric ghost is called an ''Aswang''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plant of the Month: Frangipani |url=https://daily.jstor.org/plant-of-the-month-frangipani/}}</ref>

In several Pacific islands, where plumerias were introduced in the late 19th century,{{R|ZUMBROICH|p=341}} such as [[Tahiti]], [[Fiji]], [[Samoa]], [[Hawaii]], [[New Zealand]], [[Tonga]], and the [[Cook Islands]], ''Plumeria'' species are used for making [[Lei (Hawaii)|leis]].<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.latimes.com/travel/la-tr-leis27apr27-story.html |title=  Hawaii keeps the lei-making tradition alive |author= Jay Jones |date=7 April 2008 |publisher= Los Angeles Times |access-date=7 April 2026 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260407010519/https://www.latimes.com/travel/la-tr-leis27apr27-story.html |archive-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> In Hawaii, the flower is called melia.  In modern Polynesian culture, the flower can be worn by women to indicate their relationship status—over the right ear if seeking a relationship, and over the left if taken.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.flowerleis.com/info/how-to-wear-hawaiian-flowers/ |title=How to wear Hawaiian Flowers in your hair, neck, wrist, hip and more! |website=Flower Leis |date=16 December 2015 |access-date=20 December 2015}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The page cited is not an accredited cultural authority|date=March 2026}}

''[[Plumeria rubra]]'' is the national flower of [[Laos]], where it is known under the local name ''dok champa''. It is also used as the logo of [[Lao Airlines]], the national airline of Laos.{{R|PTK}}

In eastern India and Bangladesh, plumeria is traditionally considered as a variety of the ''[[Magnolia champaca|champak]]'' flower, the ''golok chapa'', meaning the ''champaka'' that resides in the heavenly home of [[Sri Krishna]], a Hindu god at the highest realm of heaven. In Sri Lanka it is known as "Araliya" or "Temple Flower". The flower, considered sacred, is also known by the names ''gulancha'' and ''kath golap''.

In [[Culture of Bengal|Bengali culture]], most white flowers, and in particular, plumeria ([[Bengali language|Bengali]], ''chômpa'' or ''chãpa''), are associated with funerals and death.{{citation needed|date=February 2025}}

Indian incenses scented with ''[[Plumeria rubra]]'' have "''champa''" in their names. For example, ''[[nag champa]]'' is an incense containing a fragrance combining plumeria and sandalwood. While plumeria is an ingredient in Indian ''champa'' incense, the extent of its use varies between family recipes. Most ''champa'' incenses also incorporate other tree resins, such as Halmaddi (''[[Ailanthus triphysa]]'') and [[benzoin resin]], as well as other floral ingredients, including champaca (''[[Magnolia champaca]]''), geranium (''[[Pelargonium graveolens]]''), and vanilla (''[[Vanilla planifolia]]'') to produce a more intense, plumeria-like aroma.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.equinoxaromatics.com/halmaddi-ailanthus-triphysa-india.html |title=Equinox Aromatics, LLC - Halmaddi - Ailanthus triphysa - India |access-date=18 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151017231754/http://www.equinoxaromatics.com/halmaddi-ailanthus-triphysa-india.html |archive-date=17 October 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In the [[Western Ghats]] of [[Karnataka]], the bride and groom exchange garlands of cream-coloured plumeria during weddings.  Red-coloured flowers are not used in weddings in this region. Plumeria plants are found in most of the temples in these regions.

In [[East Africa|Eastern Africa]], frangipani are sometimes referred to in [[Swahili language|Swahili]] love poems.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Knappert|first1=Jan|year=1972|title=An Anthology of Swahili Love Poetry|publisher=University of California Press|page=93|isbn=0-520-02177-0}}</ref>

Some species of plumeria have been studied for their potential medicinal value.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1002/cbdv.201000159 | volume=8 | issue=8 | title=Phytochemical Constituents, Traditional Uses, and Pharmacological Properties of the Genus Plumeria | journal=  Chemistry & Biodiversity| pages=1357–1369| year=2011 | last1=Sharma | first1=Garima | last2=Chahar | first2=Maheep K. | last3=Dobhal | first3=Sonal | last4=Sharma | first4=Neelu | last5=Sharma | first5=Tek Chand | last6=Sharma | first6=Mahesh C. | last7=Joshi | first7=Yogesh C. | last8=Dobhal | first8=Mahabeer P. | s2cid=197211733 }}</ref>

=== Therapeutic and Medicinal Value ===
In Ayurvedic medicine, it is used to reduce fever, inflammation of the joints, and to relieve colic. It is also used for skin and wound care, and as an antioxidant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ask Ayurvedia: plumeria rubra |url=https://ask-ayurveda.com/wiki/article/5430-plumeria-rubra}}</ref> Furthermore, extracts from the flowers and latex have been used to treat pathogens, fungi, and bacteria. It is valued for periodontal purposes, and can be used to treat herpies, scabies, ulcers, and other skin ailments.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NIH National Library of Medicine |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9362818/}}</ref> Furthermore, traditional medicine has valued its role in diabetes treatment, as a purgative, diuretic, and even as a means of birth control.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Science Direct: Plumeria obtusa L. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667031321000348?__cf_chl_tk=RLR.OSaxhAf94tZYsVfqLPyMvU8JQ3WqaaJnA1.8Dj0-1783940537-1.0.1.1-cLAkKkqWytoqikEEy_DnhPm7LrN4BNL4Hh0rrde_9Sk}}</ref> Even its poisonous sap is used for therapeutic purposes, for stomach pains, bloating, and as a laxative.<ref>{{Cite web |title=https://daily.jstor.org/plant-of-the-month-frangipani/ |url=https://daily.jstor.org/plant-of-the-month-frangipani/}}</ref>

=== Commercial Value ===
In Vietnam, the Frangipani Club was started. Members of the club were sent to Thailand to learn about frangipani cultivation. Via cutting and grafting, flowers now grow in the country in a profusion of colours, and a variety of types, enabling farmers in the outskirts of Ho Chi Minh City to not only escape penury but to earn a handsome living, and even garner significant wealth. The plant is used nationally for landscaping in pagodas and temples, village entrances and urban environments. The demand is especially high during holidays and at expositions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Frangipani cultivation booms in Ho Chi Minh City |url=https://en.vietnamplus.vn/frangipani-cultivation-booms-in-ho-chi-minh-city-post56559.vnp}}</ref><gallery widths="200px" heights="200px">
